# Probability basics

## Sample spaces and events

A **sample space** $\Omega$ is the set of all possible outcomes of a random
experiment. An **event** $A$ is a subset of $\Omega$, i.e. $A \subseteq
\Omega$.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition: Probability measure

A probability measure $P$ on $\Omega$ satisfies:

1. $P(\Omega) = 1$
2. $P(A) \geq 0$ for all events $A$
3. For disjoint events $A_1, A_2, \dots$,
   $$
   P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} P(A_i)
   $$
:::

From these axioms it follows that for any two events $A$ and $B$,

$$
P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B).
$$ {#eq-inclusion-exclusion}

We use @eq-inclusion-exclusion repeatedly in later chapters (e.g. when
computing unions of overlapping events).

## Simulating a simple probability

Suppose we want to check the classic *birthday problem*: the probability that,
among $n$ people, at least two share a birthday. We can verify the closed-form
result with a Monte Carlo simulation in R.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
birthday_prob_sim <- function(n, trials = 10000) {
  hits <- replicate(trials, {
    birthdays <- sample(1:365, n, replace = TRUE)
    any(duplicated(birthdays))
  })
  mean(hits)
}

birthday_prob_theory <- function(n) {
  1 - prod((365 - 0:(n - 1)) / 365)
}

n_vals <- 2:50
sim <- sapply(n_vals, birthday_prob_sim)
theory <- sapply(n_vals, birthday_prob_theory)

plot(n_vals, theory, type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Number of people", ylab = "P(shared birthday)")
lines(n_vals, sim, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Theoretical", "Simulated"),
       col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), lty = c(1, 2))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Simulated vs. theoretical probability of a shared birthday](01_probability_basics_files/figure-html/birthday-sim-1.png){width=576}
:::
:::


The simulated curve tracks the theoretical curve closely, confirming the
complement-counting argument used to derive
$P(\text{no shared birthday}) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{365-i}{365}$.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exam tip

Whenever a problem asks for "at least one" of something, it's usually easier
to compute the complement $P(\text{none})$ and subtract from 1.
:::
